evidence.claim: Marcos was sworn in as the 17th President of the Philippines on June 30, 2022, and framed the start of his term around unity and sufficiency.
evidence.title: Inauguration of Ferdinand Romualdez Marcos Jr.
evidence.excerpt: Marcos was sworn in as the 17th President of the Philippines on June 30, 2022, and framed the start of his term around unity and sufficiency.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official presidential communications page for the inauguration date and office assumption.
evidence.period_fit: Exact 2022 inauguration date; directly within the ruler period.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Marcos taking office.
contrary_evidence: This is a ceremonial and self-presentational source; it does not prove policy execution.

evidence.claim: The president serves a single six-year term beginning at noon on June 30 and is not eligible for reelection, which limits prolonged personal control over existential-risk policy.
evidence.title: 1987 Philippine Constitution - The LawPhil Project
evidence.excerpt: The president serves a single six-year term beginning at noon on June 30 and is not eligible for reelection, which limits prolonged personal control over existential-risk policy.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary constitutional text establishing term length and reelection bar.
evidence.period_fit: Permanent constitutional baseline in force during 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Institutional constraint, not ruler conduct, but it shaped Marcos's available horizon.
contrary_evidence: A fixed term can still allow meaningful policy change during the term.

evidence.claim: Marcos skipped multiple journalist-led interviews and forums, and observers said he was selecting friendly outlets and trying to control the terms of engagement with the press.
evidence.title: ‘A disservice to voters’: Marcos snubs KBP, other presidential interviews to control narrative
evidence.excerpt: Marcos skipped multiple journalist-led interviews and forums, and observers said he was selecting friendly outlets and trying to control the terms of engagement with the press.
evidence.source_locator: opening paragraphs and quoted analyst commentary
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Investigative local reporting with direct commentary from media and governance observers.
evidence.period_fit: Exact 2022 campaign-period evidence before the election.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Marcos's campaign choices.
contrary_evidence: He did not avoid all media interaction outright.
The article includes critical interpretation from commentators, so the inference should stay limited to selective access and narrative control.

evidence.claim: Two Marcos campaign staffers prevented Rappler reporter Lian Buan from interviewing Marcos Jr., and a security officer shoved the reporter while a media officer pushed aside her camera.
evidence.title: Rappler journalist shoved during Uniteam rally
evidence.publisher: Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility
evidence.excerpt: Two Marcos campaign staffers prevented Rappler reporter Lian Buan from interviewing Marcos Jr., and a security officer shoved the reporter while a media officer pushed aside her camera.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent press-freedom monitor with a concrete incident and contemporaneous documentation.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Marcos's campaign environment and staff conduct.
contrary_evidence: This is a campaign incident, not a formal state policy.
It does not prove Marcos personally ordered the shove, only that his staff created the access barrier.

evidence.claim: FOCAP said Marcos supporters attacked journalists online and that reporters had difficulty getting clear and substantial answers during the campaign, with pro-Marcos content endangering and smearing independent journalists.
evidence.title: FOCAP concerned over difficulty accessing Bongbong Marcos, his supporters’ attack on journos
evidence.excerpt: FOCAP said Marcos supporters attacked journalists online and that reporters had difficulty getting clear and substantial answers during the campaign, with pro-Marcos content endangering and smearing independent journalists.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Local mainstream reporting quoting an organized press body and specific incidents.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly direct to Marcos's campaign milieu; some abuse came from supporters rather than from Marcos personally.
contrary_evidence: The report focuses on supporters and access issues, not a direct written order from Marcos.
It is evidence of the climate around the campaign, not a formal censorship mechanism.

evidence.claim: The CHR called on the Marcos administration to address attacks on journalists after death threats against TV5 reporters and after the killing of Percy Lapid, and the NUJP challenged the administration to translate its promise to protect journalists into action.
evidence.title: CHR, NUJP urge gov't to address attacks vs. journalists
evidence.excerpt: The CHR called on the Marcos administration to address attacks on journalists after death threats against TV5 reporters and after the killing of Percy Lapid, and the NUJP challenged the administration to translate its promise to protect journalists into action.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous reporting on CHR and NUJP reactions to concrete threats and a killing during Marcos's first months.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partly direct and partly inherited: it documents what the Marcos administration faced and what it had not yet demonstrably fixed.
contrary_evidence: The article shows pressure on the administration to respond, not a proven policy of repression by Marcos himself.
It is about threats and accountability rather than a formal censorship law.

evidence.claim: PCIJ reported that studies found Marcos was the main beneficiary of false or misleading content on social media and that his campaign relied on historical revisionism and narrative control.
evidence.title: Marcos leads presidential race amid massive disinformation
evidence.excerpt: PCIJ reported that studies found Marcos was the main beneficiary of false or misleading content on social media and that his campaign relied on historical revisionism and narrative control.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Investigative local reporting synthesizing fact-checking and academic work on the campaign information environment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly tied to Marcos's campaign advantage and media strategy.
contrary_evidence: The article also describes a preexisting, broader disinformation ecosystem, so not all of it is uniquely attributable to Marcos.
It is still a campaign-environment claim, not a formal state censorship claim.

unresolved_gaps: No direct 2022 Marcos-attributed existential-risk choice, safeguard reform, or command-and-control decision is recoverable.
The package is heavy on nuclear-energy framing and treaty baseline, but thin on any ruler-attributed safety or precautionary implementation.
No hard 2022 finding of personal self-enrichment, hidden assets, procurement conflict, or office misuse by Marcos is present.
Several of the strongest items are campaign-ecosystem or staffing-pattern evidence rather than clean office-period personal conduct.
